rv.q: The muffled sobs that fill the theater as the play draws to a conclusion are not elicited by cheap manipulation; they are the natural reaction to a deeply sad story dramatized with sobriety, eloquence and honesty.
They are its finest and—in a moment where truth and reconciliation can feel like utopian fantasies—its most radically hopeful.
But with just one side of the story, it’s hard to grasp how unbelievably hard it is to pull off.
Harrison’s performance aside, the play’s blows are hit and miss: connecting here, grazing there but not quite landing a proper hit.
Punch may have no physical organs but—if you’re willing to stretch the metaphor—you can say it thinks, protects, renews, breathes, and, assuredly, has a beating heart.
Punch suggests a way out, one that takes extraordinary bravery to achieve.
No description here, other than to say that its like may not be equaled on any stage this season or possibly for a few seasons to come.
Punch will linger in your memory long after you’ve left the theater, delivering grace notes of redemption that feel like a healing balm.
Clark inhabits Joan's journey as a mother contorted into outraged sorrow at Jacob's trial years before finding herself consoling him like a surrogate parent.
To that end, Punch packs a wallop.
Harrison’s volcanic yet vulnerable performance will not be forgotten by viewers – and hopefully remembered when awards season rolls around next spring.
“Punch” may falter as it trades force for feeling, but its closing moment of quiet understanding lingers like a bruise.
Will Harrison delivers an impactful performance in Broadway play inspired by real-life tragedy
If the play isn’t perfect, there is enough in “Punch” to make it feel vital.

This is an uneven production with accents flying left and right, but Graham does enough to keep a steady hand so that Joan’s struggle, generosity and open heart can be laid out by the delicate work of Clark.
This real material of a young man’s life being senselessly snuffed out resonates despite its flawed rendering; arguably a tauter and simpler retelling would have been more effective.
Most frustratingly, Punch mystifies in its primary aim: depicting the restorative justice process.
The resolution here is much too easy and pat.
That allows Punch to not only pack an emotional wallop but conclude on a note of genuine hope.
It is a wake up call that knocks us out of the park with its message: it’s never too late to be better.

cn.t: Graham's searing drama about a fatal punch and its aftermath delivers emotional power through Will Harrison's knockout debut performance, though some find its redemption narrative overly earnest or preachy despite strong staging.

vs.sum: The Samuel J. Friedman Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and a well-raked mezzanine, ensuring a clear view from most seats. The sound quality is consistently praised, and the seating is comfortable with decent legroom. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant design following renovation, though facilities like restrooms are average, leading to some congestion during intermissions.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Built-in induction loop for t-coil hearing aids.

vr.q: this show is so important... don't miss it
it culminates to a scene at the end that is sure to go down as one of the most tense and riveting scenes in the entire theatre season
Punch is currently running at MTC's Samuel J Friedman Theatre and it is really worth seeing.
This is good theater. It's well written. It's well directed and it's well performed.
